claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution, and the components inside a package inherit the package's version.
Pulumi recommends structuring the Git repositories used to publish packages per the strategies in this guide (one package per repository, cohesive components).
Following these repository-structure practices improves the reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed of the packages an organization builds and consumes.
Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
A source-based plugin package is distributed as source code in a Git repository, and the package's version is the Git tag on that repository.
Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow, typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
Publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry requires applying a semver Git tag (for example, v1.2.3) to the repository.
`pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
The `pulumi package publish` step often runs automated tests before publishing.

Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry; source-based packages referenced directly from a Pulumi.yaml file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
The version of an executable-based package is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.

A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type; a repository containing multiple packages must either release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are fine and expected, and the components ship together at the package's version.

Pulumi recommends defining exactly one package per repository, grouping a cohesive set of components inside that package, and using multiple repositories (one per package) to manage distinct packages.
The importance of the one-package-per-repository principles grows as an organization's adoption of Pulumi grows.

The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry (https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/eks/) bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with the supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
The components in the Pulumi Amazon EKS package are almost always used together and tend to evolve together, so a shared semantic version makes sense.
A single PulumiPlugin.yaml at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it in the repository.
The example repository layout places a PulumiPlugin.yaml at the repo root with components in a components/ directory (EksCluster/, EksIam/) as a single package.

Using a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components is technically possible, but Pulumi does not recommend it because it forfeits meaningful semantic versioning.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.

In a package with two unrelated components, an enhancement to ComponentA releases the package at v1.1.0 and a later breaking change to ComponentB releases it at v2.0.0, even though ComponentA had no breaking change, illustrating semver decoupling.
Splitting unrelated components across separate, right-sized packages preserves the semver contract.
The Pulumi IDP Private Registry documentation is at /docs/idp/concepts/private-registry/ and the `pulumi package publish` CLI reference is at /docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish/.
Linked pages exist: /docs/iac/concepts/packages/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, and the packaging-components page with anchors #source-based-plugin-packages and #executable-based-plugin-packages.
A Publishing packages guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/publishing-packages/ covering publishing mechanics.
